name: Alexander Acosta

summary.text: R. Alexander Acosta was the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida when his office resolved the federal investigation of Jeffrey Epstein through a 2007–2008 non-prosecution agreement, and later served as U.S. Secretary of Labor. In November 2020 the Justice Department's Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) published its review of that decision, finding that Acosta exercised poor judgment but did not commit professional misconduct.

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Professional Responsibility
sources.title: Executive Summary: Investigation into the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida's Resolution of its 2006–2008 Federal Criminal Investigation of Jeffrey Epstein

facts.claim: OPR concluded that Acosta exercised poor judgment in resolving the federal Epstein investigation through a non-prosecution agreement, but did not find that he engaged in professional misconduct.
facts.quote: OPR does not find that Acosta engaged in professional misconduct by resolving the federal investigation of Epstein in the way he did

facts.claim: OPR described the non-prosecution agreement as a flawed mechanism for satisfying the federal interest that led the government to open its investigation, while finding the decision was within Acosta's broad discretion and not driven by improper factors.
facts.quote: a flawed mechanism for satisfying the federal interest that caused the government to open its investigation of Epstein

openQuestions: The site says Acosta 'granted total immunity in 2008 stating Epstein "belonged to intelligence"'. The OPR executive summary records a non-prosecution agreement and a poor-judgment finding; it does not record any statement about intelligence. The 'belonged to intelligence' remark is attributed in press accounts to an unnamed source describing Acosta's 2017 transition interview and is not in the OPR record. The site claim is unsupported by the documents found.
The full OPR report (roughly 350 pages) was not reviewed; only the executive summary on justice.gov.
